name: cross-platform-dangerous-read-paths
description: A conservative deny baseline for third-party software with broad filesystem access. Paths are normalized to forward slashes before matching.

policy.recommended_behavior: Allow only application runtime files and files explicitly selected by the user. Apply this list as a second line of defense.
limitations: No static path list can cover every application, redirected folder, mounted volume, container, network share, or future operating-system change.
Environment variables are untrusted input. Resolve standard locations with operating-system APIs where possible.
File permissions alone do not stop screenshots, accessibility capture, clipboard access, process injection, network exfiltration, or reads performed by a privileged helper.
Rules for personal folders are deny-by-default and may be opened only through an explicit user-selected file or directory grant.
matching_requirements: Convert the candidate to an absolute path before matching.
Resolve symbolic links, junctions, aliases, mount points, short 8.3 names, and every existing parent before making the decision.
Normalize directory separators to forward slashes and collapse dot segments.
Use case-insensitive matching on Windows. On macOS, follow the actual volume case-sensitivity setting.
Expand USER_HOME once for every local account, including root, administrator, service, and currently logged-in users.
Expand list-valued variables such as KUBECONFIG into separate paths. Ignore an optional variable only when it is genuinely unset.
Treat a pattern ending in /** as matching both the directory itself and all descendants.
Reject Windows device namespaces, raw volumes, named pipes, alternate data streams, and UNC administrative shares before glob matching.
Perform the same check again immediately before opening the file to reduce time-of-check/time-of-use races.

glob_syntax.star: Matches characters inside one path segment.
glob_syntax.double_star: Matches zero or more path segments.
glob_syntax.variables: ${NAME} is expanded from a trusted operating-system-derived value before matching.

variables.USER_HOME: Every local user home resolved from the operating-system account database, not from an untrusted HOME value.
variables.APPDATA: Windows roaming application-data directory for each user.
variables.LOCALAPPDATA: Windows local application-data directory for each user.
variables.XDG_CONFIG_HOME: Linux user configuration directory; default USER_HOME/.config.
variables.XDG_DATA_HOME: Linux user data directory; default USER_HOME/.local/share.
variables.XDG_STATE_HOME: Linux user state directory; default USER_HOME/.local/state.
variables.AWS_SHARED_CREDENTIALS_FILE: Optional AWS shared credentials file override.
variables.CLOUDSDK_CONFIG: Optional Google Cloud CLI configuration-directory override.
variables.KUBECONFIG: Optional platform-separated list of Kubernetes configuration files.

dynamic_rules.source: Resolve known folders with operating-system APIs for every user account.
dynamic_rules.reason: These folders commonly contain private documents, identity records, source material, media, exports, and downloaded secrets.

dynamic_rules.source: Enumerate mounted removable media, network shares, and file-provider or cloud-sync roots with operating-system APIs.
dynamic_rules.reason: Mounted storage may expose unrelated users, backups, credentials, and synchronized private data outside the local home directory.

win32.reason: Registry hives contain local accounts, security policy, service secrets, system configuration, and per-user activity.

linux.reason: Password hashes, group authentication data, password history, and root account files.

Host keys, TLS keys, VPN secrets, Kerberos keys, and network profiles can grant machine or network identity.

Browser profiles include cookies, session tokens, saved passwords, history, autofill data, and extensions.
Mail and messaging databases can expose conversations, contacts, attachments, and active sessions.
Identity caches, domain secrets, cluster certificates, join tokens, and orchestration state can grant infrastructure access.
Swap, core dumps, authentication logs, audit trails, journals, and backups may retain credentials and historical private data.
